title: Temozolomide with short-course radiotherapy, then adjuvant treatment
context_label: Adults older than 65 with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who are not suitable for the standard radiotherapy regimen with temozolomide, under NCCP 00461.
purpose: This plan combines temozolomide with a shorter course of radiotherapy, followed by a break and adjuvant temozolomide, to help control newly diagnosed glioblastoma. NCCP identifies this particular indication as unlicensed; your team explains the evidence, alternatives and local consent process.
schedule_summary: Take temozolomide daily for 21 days during short-course radiotherapy, including weekends as prescribed. After a four-week break, take temozolomide on Days 1–5 of each 28-day cycle for up to six adjuvant cycles.
scope_note: Adults older than 65 with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who are not suitable for the standard radiotherapy regimen with temozolomide, under NCCP 00461. Use the plan matched to your diagnosis and phase; do not borrow another glioma schedule.
therapy_label: Chemotherapy and radiotherapy in separate phases
schedule_label: Take temozolomide daily for 21 days during short-course radiotherapy, including weekends as prescribed. After a four-week break, take temozolomide on Days 1–5 of each 28-day cycle for up to six adjuvant cycles.
indication_text: Adults older than 65 with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who are not suitable for the standard radiotherapy regimen with temozolomide, under NCCP 00461.
phases_note: The team confirms each phase and prescription. Do not use the capsule dose or test schedule from a different phase.
timeline_note: This 28-day view is the ADJUVANT phase only. The earlier daily chemoradiotherapy phase and four-week break are shown separately above. Symptoms can occur on any day.
safety_note: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.
teachback: Can you show the days for each medicine, the current phase, your next blood tests and whom to call for fever, vomiting or new neurological symptoms?
consent_support: Discuss treatment intent, evidence and alternatives; phase-specific schedules; blood and organ monitoring; infection, nausea, fertility and pregnancy precautions; practical support and any unlicensed use. Keep the separate radiotherapy consent and medication plans where applicable.
urgent_extra: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

agents.name: Temozolomide
agents.explanation: Temozolomide crosses into the brain and creates chemical changes in DNA. If the damage cannot be repaired, a cell may stop dividing or die. Healthy blood-forming cells can also be affected, which helps explain blood-count changes, infection and bleeding risks. Nausea prevention and liver monitoring are important too.
agents.watch: Report fever, bleeding, persistent vomiting, new breathing symptoms or yellow skin/eyes. Keep blood and liver tests even after capsule days finish.
risks: Low blood counts, infection and bleeding
Rash and rare severe skin reactions
Fertility effects and harm to a pregnancy

agents.name: Radiotherapy
agents.alias: External-beam treatment planned by radiation oncology
agents.type: Treatment focused on the brain tumour area
agents.mechanism: Damages DNA in the treated area
agents.explanation: Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.
agents.watch: Report new or worsening headache, vomiting, weakness, speech or memory change. The radiotherapy team gives a separate skin-care and symptom plan.
risks: Hair loss in the treated area
Possible delayed effects on thinking and function

passport_visit_note: Record the current phase, every prescribed medicine and treatment day, doses held, safety tests, symptoms, MRI review and the next authorised treatment. A stamp records treatment; it does not authorise the next dose.
anatomy_note: Selected regimen-specific effects use the retained detailed body illustration. Brain symptoms may come from the tumour or treatment; blood, skin and nerve effects are not confined to one point. This is not a prediction or the complete side-effect list.
anatomy: Fatigue or headache may occur. New seizures, sudden weakness, speech difficulty or loss of consciousness need emergency help.
Report mouth soreness, ulcers or reduced intake. Keep gentle mouth care and ask for help before eating or drinking becomes difficult.
Counts can fall after capsule days finish. Fever, sudden illness, bruising or bleeding needs urgent advice; keep all blood tests.
New cough, fever or breathlessness needs prompt review. Follow the prescribed PJP-prevention plan during chemoradiotherapy.
Liver injury may appear during or after treatment. Attend liver tests and report yellow skin or eyes, dark urine or unusual itching.
Take anti-sickness medicine as prescribed. Call for repeated vomiting, inability to drink, severe constipation or abdominal pain.
Follow scalp care during RT; report new rash, blisters or peeling skin. Hair loss and skin irritation depend on the treatment received.
Discuss contraception and fertility before starting. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Ask for the written medicine-specific precautions.

phases.label: Temozolomide with three weeks of radiotherapy
phases.detail: Daily capsules and scheduled radiotherapy run together. Confirm the exact final capsule day and separate PJP-prevention plan.

phases.label: Four-week break before adjuvant treatment
phases.detail: Radiotherapy has ended, but safety checks and prescribed support medicines continue. The team checks recovery before another prescription.

phases.label: Up to six adjuvant 28-day cycles
phases.detail: The first cycle has its own prescription; the team may change the dose only after reviewing tolerance and blood counts. Six cycles are the current NCCP plan.

timeline.label: Temozolomide once daily
timeline.text: Use the current phase prescription, fasting and with the prescribed nausea plan.

timeline.label: No temozolomide capsules
timeline.text: Recovery, symptoms and blood/liver tests; restart only when authorised.

timeline.label: Day 22 blood count
timeline.text: EMA recommends a count around Day 22 and follow-up until recovery.

timeline.label: Safety throughout the cycle
timeline.text: Fever, bleeding, neurological or breathing symptoms need prompt advice.

day_groups.title: Five daily capsule doses
day_groups.body: Check the prescribed capsule strengths and number each day. Take fasting with the anti-sickness plan.
day_groups.action: Do not use leftover capsules to change the dose or replace a vomited dose.

day_groups.title: No temozolomide; recovery continues
day_groups.body: Rest days allow recovery but blood counts can still fall. Continue other medicines only as individually prescribed.
day_groups.action: Contact the team for fever, sudden illness, bruising or persistent vomiting.

day_groups.title: Blood count and next-cycle decision
day_groups.body: Have the Day 22 blood count and any follow-up blood tests arranged. Before the next cycle, the team reviews counts, kidney/liver tests and symptoms.
day_groups.action: Do not start the next cycle just because the calendar reaches Day 1.

chronology_notes.title: Dose changes belong to the current phase
chronology_notes.text: Daily chemoradiotherapy and five-day cycles use different doses. Check the label and phase with the pharmacist whenever a new supply is issued.

chronology_notes.title: No replacement after vomiting
chronology_notes.text: If you vomit after a temozolomide dose, do not take a second dose that day. For a missed dose, follow the pharmacist’s written instructions or contact the team; never double up.

chronology_notes.title: Effects can be delayed
chronology_notes.text: Blood counts and liver effects can change after capsule days finish or after the last cycle. Keep the follow-up tests and emergency plan.

administration_text: Take the exact temozolomide capsule strengths and number on your pharmacy label, once daily when prescribed, on an empty stomach. Swallow whole with water; do not open, chew or crush. Ask the pharmacist to write the fasting interval and anti-sickness timing. Different phase doses are not interchangeable.

support.title: Nausea prevention
support.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. Ask what to do if nausea prevents taking medicines or fluids.

support.title: PJP infection prevention
support.text: PJP-prevention medicine is required during temozolomide with radiotherapy in this NCCP regimen. Your team supplies the prescription and decides how long to continue, including if lymphocyte counts remain low. Do not stop it just because radiotherapy has finished.

support.title: Bowels, food and fluids
support.text: Anti-sickness medicines and other medicines can worsen constipation. Ask for your bowel plan, and call for persistent vomiting, severe constipation or difficulty drinking. Do not double a dose after vomiting.

support.title: Steroid and seizure plans
support.text: Keep steroids and seizure medicines on their own written schedules if prescribed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

monitoring_summary: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and hepatitis B screening. Blood counts weekly through weeks 1–7, including four weeks after the last radiotherapy. Kidney and liver tests one and four weeks after radiotherapy. Adjuvant Day 1 blood count, kidney and liver tests each 28-day cycle; the four-week post-RT tests can form cycle 1 assessment. EMA additionally advises Day 22 blood count and after-cycle liver tests. MRI timing is individual.

monitoring_schedule.note: The team books and reviews each test. Mandatory medicine-safety checks are distinct from individually timed MRI and tumour-tissue tests. There is no universal blood tumour marker for these treatment cycles.

sections.title: Taking the treatment
sections.text: Take the exact temozolomide capsule strengths and number on your pharmacy label, once daily when prescribed, on an empty stomach. Swallow whole with water; do not open, chew or crush. Ask the pharmacist to write the fasting interval and anti-sickness timing. Different phase doses are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Missed or vomited medicine
sections.text: If you vomit after temozolomide, do not take another dose that day. For a missed dose, use your pharmacist’s written instructions or call before taking it late; do not double a dose. Never replace a dose held for toxicity.

sections.title: Medicine and supplement review
sections.text: Bring an up-to-date list of all medicines, including steroids, seizure medicines, anticoagulants, non-prescription treatments, vitamins and herbs. Ask before starting something new. Keep a record of all dose changes.

sections.title: Storage and handling
sections.text: Keep capsules in their original labelled packs, away from children. Do not open, crush or chew. If swallowing or medicine organisation is difficult, contact the team before the next dose and agree safe help. Return unused chemotherapy to the pharmacy.

sections.title: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility
sections.text: Treatment can harm a pregnancy and may affect fertility. Discuss fertility preservation, contraception for patients and partners, and the required period after the final dose before starting. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Ask the team for written, medicine-specific advice.

sections.title: Appointments and transport
sections.text: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and hepatitis B screening. Blood counts weekly through weeks 1–7, including four weeks after the last radiotherapy. Kidney and liver tests one and four weeks after radiotherapy. Adjuvant Day 1 blood count, kidney and liver tests each 28-day cycle; the four-week post-RT tests can form cycle 1 assessment. EMA additionally advises Day 22 blood count and after-cycle liver tests. MRI timing is individual.

sections.title: Help with the daily plan
sections.text: Ask a trusted person to help check the calendar if memory, vision, fatigue or hand strength makes treatment difficult. Confirm who is responsible for checking doses, collecting medicine, transport and calling for help. Keep consent and personal preferences central.

evidence.title: Perry trial: short-course radiotherapy with temozolomide in older adults
evidence.intro: A randomised study compared short-course radiotherapy alone with the addition of concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide in older adults with glioblastoma.
evidence.population: Patients aged 65 or older with newly diagnosed glioblastoma in the short-course radiation study.
evidence.interpretation: The addition of temozolomide improved survival in the study population.
limitations: The study’s age criterion and treatment duration do not replace the current Irish indication and six-cycle adjuvant plan.
An MGMT result helps discuss benefit but does not independently authorise or exclude treatment in this patient guide. Trial results do not predict individual survival.

chapters.intro: Use the regimen and phase agreed with your team.

NCCP identifies this particular indication as unlicensed; your team explains the evidence, alternatives and local consent process.

items.text: Temozolomide crosses into the brain and creates chemical changes in DNA. If the damage cannot be repaired, a cell may stop dividing or die. Radiotherapy directs high-energy radiation at the tumour and a planned surrounding area. It aims to damage tumour-cell DNA while limiting dose to nearby healthy tissue. Fatigue, scalp irritation, hair loss and swelling can occur; longer-term effects depend on the treatment area and dose.

items.title: When to seek help
items.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

items.title: Support medicines
items.text: Temozolomide has moderate-to-high oral emetic potential. Take the prescribed anti-sickness plan before chemotherapy and use rescue medicine as instructed. They are not routine medicines for every patient, and chemotherapy rest days do not automatically mean stopping them. Ask the pharmacist to check interactions.

items.title: A delay is a treatment decision
items.text: Blood counts, organ tests or symptoms may mean a dose is held, reduced or stopped. This is a safety decision, not a reason to take extra capsules later. Ask which medicines change, which support medicines continue and when the next assessment is due.

items.title: After the final dose
items.text: Agree follow-up blood tests, symptom review, MRI timing and who to contact. Continue to report new problems; effects can outlast chemotherapy. Keep your medicine list and written plan current.

chapters.title: Understanding your particular glioma
chapters.intro: Your diagnosis includes the tumour’s cells, molecular findings and behaviour, not just the word brain cancer.

items.title: The name and location
items.text: Gliomas begin in supporting cells of the brain or spinal cord. Astrocytoma, oligodendroglioma and glioblastoma are different diagnoses. A tumour that spread to the brain from another organ is a brain metastasis and is not covered by these glioma regimens. Record the exact integrated diagnosis and where it is located.

items.title: Grade is not the same as stage
items.text: Grade describes features linked to how a tumour behaves. Adult gliomas are usually discussed by their type, grade and molecular findings rather than the stage system used for many other cancers. Grade 4 does not mean cancer has spread through the body. Ask your specialist to explain your own report and any older terminology in the treatment protocol.

items.title: IDH and 1p/19q
items.text: IDH1 or IDH2 changes and loss of parts of chromosomes 1p and 19q help classify particular gliomas. The combination of findings matters: one result should not be read in isolation. These tests are usually performed on tumour tissue. They do not automatically mean a change has been inherited or that relatives need testing.

items.title: MGMT promoter methylation
items.text: MGMT is involved in repairing certain DNA damage. Methylation of its promoter can reduce that repair activity and helps the team discuss the likely benefit of temozolomide in relevant settings. It is not a blood tumour marker, a percentage of tumour left, or an individual survival prediction. Record the reported result and ask how it affects your treatment choice.

items.title: A useful diagnosis record
items.text: Keep the biopsy or operation date, pathology wording, grade, IDH result, 1p/19q result and MGMT result if tested. Mark a result as pending or not applicable rather than assuming it is negative. Ask whether specialist pathology review or further testing would change the plan.

chapters.title: Tests and scans: what each one tells you
chapters.intro: Safety blood tests, tumour tissue tests and MRI answer different questions.

items.title: Safety blood tests
items.text: A full blood count checks infection-fighting white cells, oxygen-carrying red cells and platelets that help stop bleeding. Kidney and liver tests help assess treatment safety. Attend the regimen’s required tests even when you feel well; a reassuring scan does not replace them. The schedule in this guide separates checks before, during and after treatment.

items.title: MRI and neurological review
items.text: MRI is the main scan used to assess many gliomas. Your team also considers symptoms, strength, movement, speech, memory, daily function and medicines such as steroids. Tell staff before MRI about implants or metal, kidney problems, previous contrast reactions or difficulty lying still. Ask about support if scans make you anxious.

items.title: Changes on a scan need interpretation
items.text: After treatment, inflammation and other treatment effects can resemble tumour growth on MRI. This is sometimes called pseudoprogression. The team may need comparison scans, specialist imaging or further assessment before deciding what a change means. New or worsening symptoms still need prompt review; do not assume they are harmless treatment effects.

items.title: An individual follow-up timetable
items.text: Write the next MRI date, what question it should answer and who will explain the result. Timing depends on your diagnosis, treatment phase and previous findings. General follow-up intervals in an international booklet are not automatically your schedule. These regimens do not require a generic CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or a blood tumour marker before every cycle.

items.title: Keep results with decisions
items.text: Use the passport to distinguish a test being booked, completed and reviewed. Record the agreed next step and whom to call if an appointment or result is missing. Do not alter chemotherapy or steroids yourself in response to a number or scan report.

chapters.title: Brain symptoms, medicines and when to call
chapters.intro: Symptoms may reflect the tumour, swelling, treatment, another medicine or a separate illness.

items.title: Know your usual symptoms
items.text: Write down your usual headache, strength, walking, speech, vision, memory, mood, sleep and seizure pattern before treatment. Note new changes, when they started and how they affect daily tasks. With your permission, a trusted person can help spot changes or record what happened.

items.title: Urgent neurological changes
items.text: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions.

items.title: Steroids need a separate written plan
items.text: Steroids may be prescribed to reduce swelling around the tumour. They are not automatically needed for everyone. Ask for the exact dose, time, review date and any taper plan. Do not stop or change them suddenly without advice. Report sleep or mood changes, increased thirst, infection symptoms or muscle weakness and ask which additional checks or protection you need.

items.title: Seizure medicines and rescue instructions
items.text: If prescribed, take seizure medicines on the agreed schedule. Ask what to do after a missed or vomited dose and whom to contact for breakthrough symptoms. Some medicines can affect mood, alertness or interact with treatment. Do not start, stop or switch them yourself. A rescue medicine needs an individual plan and training for whoever may give it.

items.title: Safety at home and outside
items.text: Ask your clinical team about driving, work, bathing, swimming, heights and machinery in light of your symptoms and any seizures. Local medical and licensing rules need individual advice; this guide does not give a universal driving clearance date. Occupational therapy can help adapt daily routines and the home.

chapters.title: Your overall treatment plan and choices
chapters.intro: Treatment should account for the tumour and the life you want to lead.

items.title: Understand the sequence
items.text: Surgery or biopsy, radiotherapy, chemotherapy and follow-up have different jobs. Ask your team to draw the intended sequence and identify where you are now. Concurrent treatment means treatments overlap; adjuvant treatment follows the main treatment. A change of phase may change the dose, blood tests and support medicines.

items.title: Agree what treatment is trying to achieve
items.text: Ask whether the aim is to control the tumour, delay growth, relieve symptoms, preserve function or a combination of these. Discuss likely benefits, burdens, alternatives and what would prompt a pause or stop. The answer depends on the exact diagnosis, previous treatment and your priorities.

items.title: Put evidence in context
items.text: Clinical trials describe groups of people and may use older pathology names or different schedules. They cannot predict one person’s response or lifespan. Ask how closely the evidence matches your tumour and treatment. No benefit number from one schedule should automatically be applied to another.

items.title: Discuss options available to you
items.text: Ask about appropriate clinical trials, specialist opinions, symptom support and other treatment options. A medicine or device described in an international guide is not automatically licensed, funded or suitable in Ireland. The treating multidisciplinary team explains what is available and relevant.

items.title: Make room for your priorities
items.text: Bring up fatigue, thinking, independence, family time, work, travel and side effects you most want to avoid. Ask for information at a pace and in a format that suits you. You may ask for a trusted person to join the discussion, written notes and time to reconsider decisions.

chapters.title: Living well, rehabilitation and support
chapters.intro: Practical and symptom support can begin alongside anticancer treatment.

items.title: Thinking, communication and daily tasks
items.text: Tell the team about word-finding, attention, memory, reading, vision or planning difficulties. Rehabilitation may include physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, or neuropsychological support. Written routines, rest breaks and help with medicine organisation can make day-to-day care more manageable.

items.title: Food, nausea, bowels and energy
items.text: Report poor appetite, weight change, vomiting or constipation early. Ask for dietitian help if eating is difficult. Use the prescribed anti-sickness and bowel plan; do not wait until symptoms are severe. Choose activity that is safe for your balance and strength and balance it with rest. Ask about treatable causes of fatigue.

items.title: Emotional support and carers
items.text: Anxiety, low mood, changes in behaviour and uncertainty can affect both patients and carers. Tell the team what has changed and ask for appropriate psychological or social support. Carers may need their own information, practical help and breaks. Agree who the team may share information with.

items.title: Work, transport and finances
items.text: Ask the specialist nurse or social worker about getting to treatment, time off work, benefits, caring responsibilities and support at home. Plan who can help with daily capsules and appointments if your memory, vision or fatigue makes these difficult.

items.title: Supportive care and future wishes
items.text: Supportive and palliative care can help with symptoms and quality of life while active treatment continues. You can discuss future care preferences and who you want involved in decisions at a time that suits you. Ask the team for Irish advice and documentation rather than using legal or hospice rules from a US booklet.

items.title: Information that works on paper
items.text: Keep the printed schedule, current medicine list, tests, contact numbers and emergency instructions together. This handbook can be read in sequence without internet access. The wallet card and optional QR code help others find the regimen information; they do not replace your prescription or emergency plan.

questions.q: What is my exact diagnosis, grade and relevant molecular result?
questions.a: Ask for the integrated pathology wording and an explanation of IDH, 1p/19q and MGMT where relevant. The diagnosis and treatment history guide how this regimen applies to you.

questions.q: Which phase and capsule calendar am I on now?
questions.a: Take temozolomide daily for 21 days during short-course radiotherapy, including weekends as prescribed. After a four-week break, take temozolomide on Days 1–5 of each 28-day cycle for up to six adjuvant cycles.

questions.q: What is my PJP-prevention plan, including after radiotherapy?
questions.a: The NCCP concurrent treatment requires PJP prevention. Ask which medicine, when to take it, monitoring and when the team will decide it can stop. Low lymphocyte counts may mean continuing longer.

questions.q: Which tests must happen before I can take the next dose?
questions.a: Before starting: full blood count, kidney and liver tests, glucose and hepatitis B screening. Blood counts weekly through weeks 1–7, including four weeks after the last radiotherapy. Kidney and liver tests one and four weeks after radiotherapy. Adjuvant Day 1 blood count, kidney and liver tests each 28-day cycle; the four-week post-RT tests can form cycle 1 assessment. EMA additionally advises Day 22 blood count and after-cycle liver tests. MRI timing is individual.

questions.q: Who helps with seizures, steroids, memory or daily tasks?
questions.a: Ask for a named contact, written seizure and steroid plans if prescribed, and rehabilitation or practical support. Agree who can help you organise treatment.

questions.q: Which symptoms mean contact the team today?
questions.a: Use your oncology unit’s written emergency plan. Fever, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell needs urgent advice even on days without chemotherapy. Call 112 or 999 for a new seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, loss of consciousness, severe breathing difficulty or uncontrolled bleeding. If you have an established seizure rescue plan, follow it and its emergency instructions. Contact the team promptly for a worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new cough or breathlessness, unusual bruising, yellow skin/eyes or symptoms that prevent drinking. Do not restart held chemotherapy without instructions.

questions.q: When will we review the benefit and my priorities?
questions.a: Ask for the next clinical and MRI review, how treatment effects will be distinguished from growth, and what would lead to continuing, changing or stopping treatment.

phases.title: Up to six adjuvant cycles
phases.text: Doses, starts and stopping are confirmed by the team; a card stamp is a record, not approval.

Day 1 bloods; Day 22 count and after-cycle liver tests (EMA). MRI on your plan.

cycle_expectations: The 28-day calendar is for adjuvant treatment. The earlier daily RT phase has different doses and tests.
Keep PJP prevention and other support medicines as prescribed; do not stop them automatically during the break.
preparation: Use the current pharmacy label and anti-sickness plan. Swallow capsules whole. Never double or replace a vomited dose.
patient_summary.card_schedule: Daily temozolomide with 3-week RT → 4-week break → D1–5 every 28 days, up to 6 cycles.
patient_summary.card_record_note: Six adjuvant cycle spaces; concurrent radiotherapy and recovery are separate phases. A stamp does not authorise treatment.
patient_summary.card_alert: Carry real oncology contacts and the written emergency plan. New seizures or sudden neurological changes need urgent help.

treatment_scope_notice: Adults older than 65 with newly diagnosed glioblastoma who are not suitable for the standard radiotherapy regimen with temozolomide, under NCCP 00461. This card records adjuvant cycles separately from concurrent radiotherapy.
